clue.text: Piss about with substitute Eye

parts.note: to piss is to pee, crudely put

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the stand-in's short name is read backwards

parts.note: a rep, short for representative, is someone who stands in for and acts on behalf of another

explanation.surface: A crude order to stop messing around and let a stand-in take over the Eye, Private Eye's own nickname for itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eye' looks like the magazine, Private Eye, but it is simply the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A peeper is an informal word for an eye, the thing one peeps through.

clue.text: Be better to flog said old flame first?

indicators.note: first sends the former lover to the front of the answer

parts.note: an ex is a former lover

indicators.note: said tells us to take the word for flog by its sound alone

parts.note: to flog something is British slang for to sell it

explanation.surface: A vindictive question: would it be better to sell off your ex-lover first?
explanation.walkthrough: 'flog' suggests a whipping, but in British slang it means to sell.
explanation.definitionFit: To excel is to surpass others, to do better than them.

clue.text: Unidentified correspondent gets piss-pot, pisspoor pension

parts.note: a po is a chamber pot

indicators.note: pisspoor means very bad, so the word pension is in a bad state and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An anonymous letter writer complains of receiving a miserable pension and a chamber pot.
explanation.walkthrough: PO, from the French pot, is a British word for a chamber pot.
explanation.definitionFit: A poison pen writes malicious anonymous letters, so is an unnamed correspondent.

clue.text: Mug on old jerk like a Dalek

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above the following letters

parts.note: to mug someone is to rob them in the street
a tic is an involuntary twitch or jerk

explanation.surface: A thug mugs an old man with a twitch, as mechanically as a Dalek.
explanation.walkthrough: Daleks are the robotic alien villains of the BBC science fiction series Doctor Who.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dalek is a mechanical, machine-like creature, so behaving like one is acting in the manner of a robot.

clue.text: Perverse American copies drunken bums and dies

indicators.note: perverse in its root sense of turned the wrong way, so the short word for American is reversed

parts.note: cc stands for carbon copies on a letter

indicators.note: drunken letters stagger out of order, so bums is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lurid tabloid line about a deviant American, imitations of sozzled tramps, and a death.
explanation.walkthrough: CC is the 'carbon copies' line at the foot of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To succumb is to give way, and in particular to give way to illness or injury and die.

clue.text: Ungenuine bastard! — small British crooked firm of greedy, silky representatives

indicators.note: crooked means bent out of shape, so these letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the two words supply most of the letters to be rearranged
small says shorten British to its abbreviation

explanation.surface: A furious outburst at a phoney rogue, followed by a dig at a dodgy little British law firm.
explanation.walkthrough: Sue, Grabbit and Runne is Private Eye's invented firm of rapacious libel lawyers; a silk is a senior barrister, a Queen's Counsel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eye's fictional legal practice stands for greedy lawyers in silk gowns who represent clients for huge fees.

clue.text: Calm down leader of Conservatives — stupid fool without ministry backing

indicators.note: leader of takes just the first letter of Conservatives

parts.note: the word's first letter is taken

indicators.note: without in the old sense of outside, so the muddled letters go around the department
stupid suggests the word fool is muddled, so its letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be mixed up

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the abbreviation is reversed

parts.note: FO is the Foreign Office, a government ministry

explanation.surface: Telling a Tory leader to calm down: he is a fool with no government department behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like lacking, but here means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: To cool off is to let one's anger subside, to become calmer.

clue.text: Sun: "Topless Peg — Free!"

indicators.note: topless removes the top, the first letter, of the newspaper's name

parts.note: the name of the British tabloid newspaper, taken as written
a pin is a peg used to fasten things

explanation.surface: A Sun headline with its trademark topless Page 3 model, a girl called Peg, offered free.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is the British tabloid famous for its topless Page 3 photographs.
explanation.definitionFit: To unpin something is to release it by removing its fastening, which sets it free.

clue.text: No intellectual but will make large organ stiff

definitions.note: adjectival here: of a person who is no intellectual

parts.note: the brain is one of the body's largest organs
a stiff is slang for a corpse, so someone dead

explanation.surface: A smutty joke: an unbrainy man boasts what will give him an erection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'large organ stiff' plays on a sexual reading; the organ is the brain and stiff means dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone brain-dead is a slang insult for being utterly stupid, the opposite of clever.

clue.text: Bell's out (long gone), about to nick someone else's piece — that's to be a hack

indicators.note: about means going around, so the jumbled letters surround the copying word
out signals the letters are put out of their order
gone says the letter for long has left the word

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large or long
to crib is to copy another person's work, as a schoolchild does

explanation.surface: A jumble of journalism grumbling: a contributor has left, and someone is plagiarising articles, which is what hacks do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'piece' suggests a chess man or a gun, but it is a piece of writing; to crib is to copy one. 'that's to' just joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A hack is a poor-quality writer, and to scribble is to write hastily and carelessly, as such a writer does.

clue.text: Oprah outburst at end of transmission: "Kill mom and dad!"

definitions.note: a verb phrase: to orphan a child is to take away its parents

indicators.note: an outburst bursts the name apart, so its letters are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: the talk-show host's first name, taken as written

indicators.note: end of picks out the last letter of transmission

parts.note: its last letter is taken

explanation.surface: A talk-show host loses control at the close of the broadcast and screams for her parents to be killed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kill mom and dad' reads as Oprah's own shout, but it defines the verb: to leave a child without parents.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to orphan someone is to deprive a child of both parents, typically by their death.

clue.text: Disagree on going topless, giving the full monty

indicators.note: a topless word has lost its top, that is its first letter

parts.note: to fall out is to quarrel or disagree

explanation.surface: A row about whether to strip to the waist ends with someone stripping completely.
explanation.walkthrough: The full monty is British slang for everything, the whole lot; it is also the film title for stripping naked. 'on' just links the two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: An all-out effort holds nothing back, just as giving the full monty means giving absolutely everything.

clue.text: Injured a groin? No good making sexy noises

indicators.note: injured letters are damaged and knocked into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man hurts himself in the groin, and the noises he makes are not the pleasurable kind.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface wants the groans to be pain; the definition reads them as sounds of pleasure.
explanation.definitionFit: Groaning is uttering low moaning sounds, which can be cries of pleasure during sex as well as of pain.

clue.text: See 5
It'll come as no shock to its victims

definitions.meaning: reads as something unsurprising, but a shock is also a thick mass of hair
the sufferers of a condition, here one that leaves them with no hair

explanation.walkthrough: 'shock' looks like surprise, but a shock of hair is a thick head of it, which this condition takes away.
explanation.definitionFit: Alopecia is the medical term for hair loss, leaving its sufferers bald or patchy-haired.

clue.text: It'll age us terribly, such action!

indicators.note: terribly means badly, so the letters come out badly arranged

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A weary complaint that court proceedings will make everyone old before their time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'action' here is a legal action, a lawsuit, which famously drags on for years.
explanation.definitionFit: In law an action is a case brought before a court, which is exactly what a lawsuit is.

clue.text: Leader reported "Eff you, Royal Highness arsyversy Brenda!"

indicators.note: reported means spoken aloud, so the two words are taken by their sound as letters

parts.note: the spoken words sound like the letters F and U

indicators.note: arsy-versy is old slang for back to front, so the abbreviation is reversed

parts.note: RH is the abbreviation in HRH, His or Her Royal Highness
Private Eye's long-standing nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, whose royal cipher was ER

explanation.surface: A political leader is quoted swearing at the Queen in the crudest terms, as Private Eye might report.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls the Queen 'Brenda'; her cipher ER stands for Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: Führer is the German word for leader, notoriously the title taken by Hitler.

clue.text: Stockings fastened to organ feature facilitate passing of water

definitions.note: a verb phrase describing what the answer, a plural noun, does

parts.note: hose is an old word for stockings
an organ makes its sound through pipes

explanation.surface: Stockings attached to a body part to help with urination, a lavatorial image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passing water' suggests urinating; the definition is about garden hoses carrying water.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosepipes are flexible tubes for carrying water from a tap, for instance to a garden.

clue.text: Discussions of this country go with a bang?

definitions.meaning: Private Eye's long-running coy phrase for sex names discussions about an African nation, after a 1970s party story
sounds like an event that is a great success, but means ending in sex

explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye readers know 'Ugandan discussions' as the magazine's coy phrase for sexual intercourse, coined after a journalist claimed to be discussing Ugandan affairs upstairs at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: The country is the East African state whose name was borrowed for the Eye's running euphemism for sexual activity.

clue.text: Gold knockers put upon foreign residential placements?

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
knockers is slang for breasts, which come in pairs

explanation.surface: Golden breasts adorning young foreigners who are exploited in their host families.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put upon' describes the au pairs, often exploited as cheap help, and leads into the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Au pairs are young people from abroad who live with a host family and help in the home.

clue.text: Relapse into sin? Not Labour's leader, the arse!

indicators.note: not here means without, so a letter is dropped from the word for relapsing

parts.note: to backslide is to fall back into sin or bad habits

indicators.note: Labour's leader is the first letter of Labour

parts.note: its first letter is taken

explanation.surface: An outburst at a lapsed politician: he has gone back to his old ways, and he is no Labour leader, the idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour's leader' looks like a party figure such as Blair, but it gives only an L.
explanation.definitionFit: Backside is a familiar word for the buttocks, which is what the arse means in British slang.

clue.text: Barnet a bit spiky with sailors wanting a slash

parts.note: a ship's crew is its sailors
a cut is a slash with a blade

explanation.surface: Seamen who need to urinate, a slash being British slang for that, sporting spiky hair.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet is Cockney rhyming slang for hair (Barnet Fair); 'a slash' suggests urinating but means a cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A crew cut is a very short, bristly men's haircut, so the hair stands up in spikes.

clue.text: Top shelf screwing in strip club?

indicators.note: screwing twists things around, so these letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Top-shelf magazines, the soft porn kept high in newsagents, being acted out in a strip club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top shelf' is British shorthand for pornographic magazines, kept out of children's reach.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleshpot is a place offering sensual pleasures and vice, of which a strip club is an example.

clue.text: Girl is over being grabbed by MacGregor

indicators.note: being grabbed means held inside, so the turned word sits within the presenter's first name

parts.note: Sue MacGregor, long-serving presenter of BBC Radio 4's Today programme

indicators.note: over means turned over, so is is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: A girl is past being groped by a man called MacGregor.
explanation.walkthrough: MacGregor looks like a man's surname, but it is the broadcaster Sue MacGregor.
explanation.definitionFit: Susie is a female first name, the kind of name a clue calls simply a girl.

clue.text: Cyclops in Pyrex-dished death

indicators.note: in puts the setter's letter inside the jumbled brand name
dished means ruined or smashed, so the dish brand's letters are broken up

parts.note: the glassware brand name, taken as written
the setter's pseudonym; a Cyclops has one eye, and the setter means me, I

explanation.surface: The setter meets a grim end in an ovenproof dish, Pyrex being a brand of heat-resistant glassware.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's name in a clue usually stands for I or ME; this one, Cyclops, also suggests a single eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Expiry means coming to an end, and in older or formal use the end of life itself.

clue.text: See 5
Emasculated religious adherent gobbles English breakfast?

indicators.note: gobbles means swallows up, so the shortened word takes a letter inside it
emasculated means losing the male, so the M for male is removed

parts.note: a follower of Islam

explanation.surface: A castrated believer wolfing down a full English breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the standard abbreviation for male, so emasculating a word removes an M.
explanation.definitionFit: Muesli is a Swiss mixture of oats, nuts and dried fruit eaten as a breakfast cereal.

clue.text: Convicted tax dodger gives head inside lacking company

indicators.note: inside places the short word for head within the word for solitary

parts.note: being alone is being without company
to cap is to top or head something, as a cap sits on the head

explanation.surface: A jailed tax cheat offers sexual favours to fellow inmates because he is lonely.
explanation.walkthrough: Al Capone, the Chicago gangster, was finally jailed in 1931 for tax evasion rather than for his violent crimes.
explanation.definitionFit: The notorious Prohibition mobster was convicted not of murder or bootlegging but of evading income tax.

clue.text: See 5
Drove home more than half pissed after rest collapsed

indicators.note: after puts the letters from the drunken word behind the jumbled ones
collapsed letters fall down and land in a different order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged
four of the six letters of pissed, its last four

explanation.surface: Someone drove home thoroughly drunk after their rest gave way to collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drove home' tempts a reading about driving; it means emphasised, as in driving a point home.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive a point home is to insist on it forcefully, which is to have stressed it.

clue.text: Shy Brenda? Bull!

definitions.note: a noun: a bull tosses people on its horns, so it is literally a tosser

parts.note: to shy is to throw, as at a coconut shy, and to toss is likewise to throw
Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, whose cipher was ER

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at the Queen for being shy and dismisses the idea as nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: A bull tosses with its horns; 'tosser' is also British slang for a contemptible person, which the exclamation suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken literally, a bull is an animal that throws people into the air with its horns, so it is one who tosses.
